rv.q: Its stint in the West End is a joyous reprise of that first production with all the inessentials thrown in (including soft bread rolls flung into the stalls – I’ve never been at a show so exuberantly full of missiles).
This adaptation by the poet James Fenton of Miguel de Cervantes’s novel is a delight.
In a production this joyful, it's tremendously fun to watch him try.
The persistence of Threlfall and co works its own rough magic.
It’s a moment of childish release that is symptomatic of this joyous show, which brings Miguel de Cervantes’s misguided knight to the stage with a mixture of mischief and affection.
Though some of the earlier silly business smacks of enforced fun, the production gradually grows into something stronger and subtler, anchored by the two central performances.
The first half has an anarchic verve that's close to pantomime — including a food fight that sees the stalls pelted with bread rolls.
With a lively script by James Fenton and lovely songs, it compresses the 1,000-page sprawl of Cervantes's novel into a tight 2 ½ hours.
Angus Jackson’s joyous production will bring great pleasure to anyone lucky enough to procure a ticket, whether or not they are fans of the original.
This is fine, quality fun, big-hearted and innately theatrical.
In short, the RSC has a winning West End Christmas show for all the family.
The RSC's version starring David Threlfall is handsomely designed but dramatically weightless.

cn.t: Critics praise the RSC's joyous, entertaining adaptation of Cervantes' sprawling novel, with David Threlfall's dedicated performance and James Fenton's nimble script earning acclaim, though one dissenter finds it dramatically weightless.
